To understand factors determining such resistance-associated cell wall alterations, we train a random forest regression model on the PGNet solution space, from which we identify ddl as the most influential factor impacting cell wall synthesis, in addition to mraY and murA . Based on these insights, we demonstrate that a combination of vancomycin and d-cycloserine (Ddl-inhibitor), or alternatively, fosfomycin (MurA-inhibitor), significantly retards the emergence of vancomycin-resistance in a clinical MRSA strain.

title: Alterations in the Ser/Thr phosphatase StpA confer van-independent reduced susceptibility to dalbavancin in Enterococcus faecium
abstract: Dalbavancin is a long-acting lipoglycopeptide increasingly used against difficult-to-treat Gram-positive infections, including enterococcal infections. However, mechanisms conferring reduced susceptibility in Enterococcus faecium remain uncharacterized. We selected in vitro spontaneous mutants with decreased susceptibility to dalbavancin in two distinct vancomycin-susceptible E. faecium backgrounds and identified independent missense mutations in the flap domain of the Ser/Thr phosphatase StpA. Deletion of stpA increased dalbavancin MICs, and complementation with the wild-type allele restored susceptibility, linking StpA to the reduced-susceptibility phenotype. Mutants displayed reduced cell size, thicker cell wall enriched in 3-3 cross-links, concentration-dependent reduction of dalbavancin binding, elevated levels of MurA and other envelope-biosynthesis proteins, and global hyperphosphorylation of several cell-division regulators. Despite only a modest increase in MIC, dalbavancin’s in vivo efficacy was abolished in a Galleria mellonella model. These findings suggest that StpA-dependent envelope remodeling represents an original pathway for reducing susceptibility to dalbavancin in E. faecium independent of canonical van -mediated resistance.

title: LLM-powered construction of antibiotic resistance datasets and knowledge graphs for accelerated antibiotic resistance gene discovery
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a mounting global public health and development threat, with the misuse and overuse of antibiotics driving the rapid dissemination of multidrug-resistant pathogens. Developing next-generation small-molecule antibiotics requires in-depth investigation of resistance mechanisms and the identification of novel targets to overcome the limitations of current treatments. However, current strategies mainly rely on sequence-based homology search or models trained on manually curated datasets, which often suffer from outdated annotations, limited coverage, and high false-positive rates. These limitations hinder the identification of novel resistance targets. To address these limitations, we developed a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered automated pipeline that systematically mines resistance-related knowledge from full-text publications and supplementary materials, thereby supporting scalable and iterative data integration. Building on this framework, we constructed AResDB , a curated resource that integrates data from over 8570 published papers covering bacterial species, compounds, genes, mutations, phenotypes, and quantitative measurements. On this foundation, we constructed AResKG , a large-scale, multi-species knowledge graph of antibiotic resistance integrating 14 entity types, 27 relation types, and over 52.1 million triples. Experimental results based on AResKG demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of commonly used machine learning methods for predicting gene-antibiotic resistance, compared with existing knowledge graphs. This work establishes a scalable, LLM-powered framework for antibiotic resistance research that advances the understanding of resistance mechanisms and accelerates the discovery of next-generation therapeutics.

title: Sublethal colistin exposures prime multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens for enhanced predation by Bdellovibrio
abstract: Predatory bacteria offer a distinct strategy against antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative pathogens, but their interactions with antibiotics remain poorly defined. Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus HD100 remained viable during colistin exposure and synergized with colistin against mcr-1 -positive Escherichia coli . At 8 mg/L colistin and a predator-to-prey ratio of approximately 1.5, combination treatment produced a 6.75-log reduction in viable prey by 6 h, reduced counts below detection by 24 h, and depleted qPCR-detectable mcr-1 abundance by 99.96%. Transient colistin pretreatment increased HD100 attachment twofold and bdelloplast formation 1.56-fold. Colistin increased prey outer-membrane permeability without detectable inner-membrane disruption, whereas polymyxin B nonapeptide, a markedly weaker bactericide, reproduced the predation-enhancing effects. Potentiation extended to Gram-negative pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii . In Galleria mellonella , combination treatments increased day-3 survival to 50%, compared with 0%, 8.3%, and 16.7% for untreated, colistin, and HD100 groups, respectively. These findings define antibiotic-facilitated predation as a strategy exploiting residual antibiotic activities against pathogens.

title: What are the roles of sex and gender in antimicrobial resistance? Evidence across infection, selection and transmission
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is shaped by biosocial and microbiological processes, yet sex and gender have not been systematically framed across the three domains (infection, antibiotic selection and transmission) that lead to drug-resistant infection. Synthesising available evidence, we find no consistent sex or gender bias in resistance prevalence; where differences are reported, prevalence is more often higher in men. Context-specific analyses are needed to determine how gendered interventions should be, if at all.

title: Antimicrobial use contributes to resistance gene enrichment across cattle groups on commercial dairy farms
abstract: Antimicrobial use (AMU) in agricultural systems is frequently linked to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Yet, the scale at which AMU reshapes host‑associated resistomes remains unclear. This gap arises, in part, from the scarcity of farm‑level AMU data from commercial production systems. Here, we combine detailed AMU records from commercial dairy farms with metagenomic analyses of bovine fecal resistomes from calves, healthy lactating adult cows, sick cows, and cull cows. Across all farms, resistome profiles were similar regardless of overall AMU. Resistance associated with historically common antibiotics, such as tetracyclines, was frequent on low‑ and high‑AMU farms, indicating that some resistance classes are ubiquitous in dairy systems regardless of historical AMU. In contrast, resistance to specific drug classes varied systematically with AMU. Higher AMU was associated with increased resistance to aminoglycosides, β‑lactams, and macrolides, drug classes that are critical for treating mastitis and bovine respiratory disease. Resistance gene richness and diversity were highest in calves, underscoring the importance of accounting for host traits alongside AMU when evaluating resistance patterns. Together, these findings underscore the need for detailed, farm‑level AMU data to understand how management practices shape AMR and to inform strategies for sustaining the effectiveness of existing antimicrobials in agricultural and public‑health contexts.

title: Characterization of a novel topoisomerase inhibitor (NBTI) with broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, including mycobacterial pathogens
abstract: Resistance to fluoroquinolone antibiotics is rising across bacterial pathogens, including the important pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ), posing a major threat to global health. Novel bacterial topoisomerase inhibitors (NBTIs) can overcome fluoroquinolone resistance. However, the only FDA-approved NBTI, the triazaacenaphthylene compound gepotidacin, is not indicated for mycobacterial infections. Here we characterize compound B1 , a previously identified NBTI with broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, including against Gram-negative clinical isolates and the mycobacterium Mtb . B1 selectively inhibited prokaryotic topoisomerases, including Mtb gyrase, with greater potency than the FDA-approved NBTI gepotidacin. Consistent with the NBTI mode of action, B1 primarily induced single-strand DNA breaks, and structural studies revealed binding within the NBTI pocket of gyrase. B1 showed enhanced efficacy against Mtb in broth culture and in an ex-vivo Mtb macrophage infection model compared with gepotidacin. In zebrafish embryos, B1 cleared infections with clinical isolates of Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii , but—like gepotidacin—was inactive against Mycobacterium marinum . Although well tolerated in vivo, B1 strongly inhibited the human ether-à-go-go (hERG) channel, indicating a cardiotoxicity risk. Together, our findings position B1 as a promising NBTI scaffold for anti(myco)bacterial drug development, requiring optimization to overcome hERG liability and enable in vivo studies in an appropriate Mtb infection model.

title: Hfc-mediated enhancement of plasmid conjugation drives the dissemination of carbapenem-resistant hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: The horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) plasmids drives the global spread of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Among these, carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP), particularly high-risk hypervirulent lineages (CR-hvKP), poses a major clinical threat due to the rapid dissemination of resistance determinants. However, the mechanisms underlying efficient plasmid transmission in these high-risk clones remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Hfc, a plasmid-encoded factor that enhances conjugative transfer in K. pneumoniae . Genomic epidemiological analyses revealed that hfc is widely distributed, predominantly associated with conjugative IncF-type plasmids, highly enriched in the ST11-KL64, the predominant epidemic CR-hvKP lineage, and has increased in prevalence alongside the recent expansion of this high-risk clone. Functional studies demonstrated that deletion of hfc markedly reduced plasmid transfer efficiency, whereas its overexpression enhanced conjugation in vitro and promoted plasmid dissemination during mouse gut colonization. Mechanistically, Hfc was found to bind the plasmid origin of transfer ( oriT ) and is associated with increased expression of a subset of T4SS-related genes, as well as enhanced pilus-like structures and elevated intracellular ROS levels. In addition, Hfc shows potential interaction with TraC, a VirB4-like ATPase involved in T4SS assembly and activity, suggesting a possible role in modulating conjugation machinery function. Notably, Hfc imposes no detectable fitness or virulence cost on the host. Together, these findings identify Hfc as a conserved enhancer of plasmid conjugation and a potential target for limiting the spread of AMR plasmids in high-risk CR-hvKP lineages.

title: Temporal dynamics drive soil resistome variation more strongly than warming or biocide application
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a major global health concern. Understanding how climate change-related factors can influence antimicrobial resistance patterns in the environment is essential for developing efficient One Health-based resistance control strategies. In this study, under field conditions, we assessed the combined effects of soil warming and biocide (herbicide, fungicide, insecticide) application on soil physicochemical and microbial parameters, potato yield, and the soil resistome using the targeted metagenomics ResCap platform to quantify antimicrobial resistance genes (i.e., antibiotic resistance genes, metal resistance genes, biocide resistance genes, relaxase genes). To our knowledge, this is the first field study specifically designed to investigate the effects of the interaction between agricultural practices (i.e., biocide application) and soil temperature on the environmental resistome, thereby providing insight into the potential contribution of agroecosystems to the reported link between rising air temperatures and the increasing prevalence of antibiotic resistance. Our results indicate that neither soil warming nor biocide application were key factors affecting the observed variation in the abundance of resistance genes. Instead, temporal dynamics during the growing season had the strongest influence on the soil resistome, with the initial manure application likely contributing to the observed temporal patterns. These findings highlight the importance of studying the temporal dynamics during the growing season when evaluating how agricultural practices and climate change-related factors can influence the environmental resistome.
